hold_back: 10/9 is more than 3/5, because 3/5 is less than 1 and 10/9 is more than 1, so 3/5 < 10/9

media.teaching_notes: Predict first: which is more, 3/5 or 10/9? You do not need to cut anything. Where does each fraction sit compared with 1? 1 is a signpost on the number line. 3/5 is 3 pieces of 1/5, and 5 pieces would make 1, so 3/5 is less than 1. 10/9 is 10 pieces of 1/9, and 9 pieces already make 1, so 10/9 is more than 1. 3/5 is to the left of 1 and 10/9 is to the right of 1. A fraction to the left of 1 is less than a fraction to the right of 1, so 3/5 < 10/9. If both fractions are more than 1, then 1 cannot decide. Write each as a whole number and a part and compare the whole numbers first. Rule: check each fraction against 1. A fraction less than 1 is less than a fraction more than 1. 1. 3/5 is 3 pieces of 1/5. 5 pieces of 1/5 make 1, and 3 is less than 5, so 3/5 is less than 1. 2. 10/9 is 10 pieces of 1/9. 9 pieces of 1/9 make 1, and 10 is more than 9, so 10/9 is more than 1. 3. 3/5 is on the left of 1 on the number line and 10/9 is on the right of 1. 4. A fraction less than 1 is less than a fraction more than 1, so 3/5 < 10/9. 5. Check: 3/5 + 2/5 = 5/5 = 1, so 3/5 falls short of 1, and 10/9 = 1 + 1/9 goes past 1. Answer: 10/9 is more than 3/5, because 3/5 is less than 1 and 10/9 is more than 1, so 3/5 < 10/9
media.instructions_for_student: When the video says think and tell, say your answer out loud. Then watch how the book's example is solved.

content.text:
1. Predict first: which is more, 3/5 or 10/9? You do not need to cut anything. Where does each fraction sit compared with 1?
2. 1 is a signpost on the number line. 3/5 is 3 pieces of 1/5, and 5 pieces would make 1, so 3/5 is less than 1.
3. 10/9 is 10 pieces of 1/9, and 9 pieces already make 1, so 10/9 is more than 1.
4. 3/5 is to the left of 1 and 10/9 is to the right of 1. A fraction to the left of 1 is less than a fraction to the right of 1, so 3/5 < 10/9.
5. If both fractions are more than 1, then 1 cannot decide. Write each as a whole number and a part and compare the whole numbers first.
6. Rule: check each fraction against 1. A fraction less than 1 is less than a fraction more than 1.

content.text:
Worked example: Which is more, 3/5 or 10/9? Use 1 as the reference.
1. 3/5 is 3 pieces of 1/5. 5 pieces of 1/5 make 1, and 3 is less than 5, so 3/5 is less than 1.
2. 10/9 is 10 pieces of 1/9. 9 pieces of 1/9 make 1, and 10 is more than 9, so 10/9 is more than 1.
3. 3/5 is on the left of 1 on the number line and 10/9 is on the right of 1.
4. A fraction less than 1 is less than a fraction more than 1, so 3/5 < 10/9.
5. Check: 3/5 + 2/5 = 5/5 = 1, so 3/5 falls short of 1, and 10/9 = 1 + 1/9 goes past 1.
Answer: 10/9 is more than 3/5, because 3/5 is less than 1 and 10/9 is more than 1, so 3/5 < 10/9

Worked example: Compare each fraction with 1/2. Is it equal to, less than or more than 1/2? (a) 9/18 (b) 7/15

5. Check: 2 × 9 = 18, so 9/18 is exactly half. 2 × 7 = 14, and 14 is less than 15, so 7/15 is less than half.
Answer: (a) 9/18 = 1/2 (b) 7/15 is less than 1/2

Row one shows 'Same whole' with two squares, 'Fraction of a grid' with six blue squares in a 48-square grid, and 'Pieces make a whole' combining parts into '1/2 + 1/4 + 1/4 = 1'. media.teaching_notes: Walk the counter in reading order and ask the child to say one idea at each card, then to find one card they would still like to try. Do not add numbers to the panels; the pictures are only reminders.

topics.summary: The chapter's ideas in one walk through the kitchen: the same whole, fractions of a grid, making a whole from pieces, equivalent fractions, comparing with the same denominator, the same numerator, with 1 and with 1/2, fractions greater than 1, and the relations puzzle.

content.text:
1. Predict first: you have walked through the whole kitchen of fractions. Can you say one idea from each stop, from the two chocolates to the puzzle? Read the lines below and tick each idea you remembered.
2. Same whole: two fractions can be compared only when they are parts of the same whole. 1/3 of a big chocolate can be more than 1/2 of a small one.
3. Check: the small chocolate has 4 blocks and the big one has 9 blocks, all blocks the same size. 1/2 of the small one is 4 ÷ 2 = 2 blocks and 1/3 of the big one is 9 ÷ 3 = 3 blocks. The third of the big chocolate is more.
4. Fraction of a grid: split the squares into equal groups, and one group is the fraction. A grid of 48 squares has 48 ÷ 8 = 6 squares in 1/8 and 48 ÷ 6 = 8 squares in 1/6.
5. Making a whole: 5 pieces of 1/5 make 5/5 = 1. Pieces of different sizes make a whole too, such as 1/2 + 1/4 + 1/4 = 1.
6. Equivalent fractions name the same part of a whole with different names: 1/3 = 2/6 = 3/9 = 4/12. Cut every part into more equal parts and the top and bottom numbers grow by the same number of times.
7. Check: 2/5 = 6/15. Top and bottom both grew 3 times, because 2 × 3 = 6 and 5 × 3 = 15.
8. Same denominator: count the pieces. 2/3 is more than 1/3 because 2 pieces of 1/3 are more than 1 piece of 1/3.
9. Same numerator: look at the size of one piece. 4/5 is more than 4/6 because a 1/5 piece is bigger than a 1/6 piece.
10. Check: which is more, 3/8 or 3/7? 3/7, because a 1/7 piece is bigger than a 1/8 piece.
11. Fractions greater than 1: 5 pieces of 1/2 make 5/2 = 2 1/2 and 9 pieces of 1/4 make 9/4 = 2 1/4. A fraction is greater than 1 when its top number is more than its bottom number.
12. Check: how many parathas are 8 pieces of 1/4? 8/4 = 2 parathas, because 8 ÷ 4 = 2.
13. Compare with 1: a fraction below 1 is less than a fraction above 1. 7/8 is less than 1 and 8/6 is more than 1, so 7/8 < 8/6.
14. Compare with 1/2: a fraction is equal to 1/2 when its top is half of its bottom, like 4/8 and 3/6. 5/8 is more than 1/2 and 3/6 is half, so 5/8 > 3/6.
15. Check: is 3/15 more or less than 1/2? Less, because half of 15 is more than 3.
16. Ants: 16 ants, each 1/4 cm long, make 16 × 1/4 = 16/4 = 4 cm.
17. Puzzle: follow a relation one link at a time. The only brother of your father's sister is your father, so his child is your brother or sister.

modules.module_summary: Comparing fractions with 1 and with 1/2 as references, a puzzle about family relations, and a revision of the whole kitchen of fractions.

objectives.strand_name: Same Whole, Equal Parts and Equivalent Fractions
objectives.objective_text: Students explain that a fraction is a part of its own whole and compare two fractions only when the wholes are the same size.

objectives.strand_name: Same Whole, Equal Parts and Equivalent Fractions
objectives.objective_text: Students explain why 1/3 of a big chocolate can be more than 1/2 of a small one, and say that two fractions can be compared only when they are parts of the same whole.

objectives.strand_name: Same Whole, Equal Parts and Equivalent Fractions
objectives.objective_text: Students find 1/n of a grid by sharing its squares into n equal groups and counting the squares in one group.

objectives.strand_name: Same Whole, Equal Parts and Equivalent Fractions
objectives.objective_text: Students show that small equal parts can join to cover the same area as a bigger fraction of a grid, and name that area with both fractions.

objectives.strand_name: Same Whole, Equal Parts and Equivalent Fractions
objectives.objective_text: Students shade 1/8, 1/6 and 1/12 of a 48-square grid by sharing the squares into equal groups, and mark where 1/3 appears.

objectives.strand_name: Same Whole, Equal Parts and Equivalent Fractions
objectives.objective_text: Students make a whole with pieces of one size and say how many pieces of 1/n are needed to fill it.

objectives.strand_name: Same Whole, Equal Parts and Equivalent Fractions
objectives.objective_text: Students make a whole with pieces of different sizes and write two names for the same part as equivalent fractions.

objectives.strand_name: Same Whole, Equal Parts and Equivalent Fractions
objectives.objective_text: Students find how many small pieces fit in a bigger piece by counting the small pieces that cover it, and write the two names of that part.

objectives.strand_name: Same Whole, Equal Parts and Equivalent Fractions
objectives.objective_text: Students find equivalent fractions, find how many small pieces fit in a bigger piece, and make wholes with pieces of one size and of different sizes.

objectives.strand_name: Same Whole, Equal Parts and Equivalent Fractions
objectives.objective_text: Students cut every part of a shaded shape into more equal pieces, write the new fraction, and explain that the shaded part stays the same while the fraction gets a different name.

objectives.strand_name: Same Whole, Equal Parts and Equivalent Fractions
objectives.objective_text: Students describe the pattern in a list of equivalent fractions, say that the top number and the bottom number are multiplied by the same number, and use it to write a new equivalent fraction.

objectives.strand_name: Same Whole, Equal Parts and Equivalent Fractions
objectives.objective_text: Students write fractions equivalent to a given fraction by cutting shapes into equal parts, tick the pairs that are equivalent, and fill in the missing top or bottom number to make two fractions equivalent.

objectives.strand_name: Comparing Fractions and Going Past One
objectives.objective_text: Students compare two fractions that have the same denominator by counting the pieces of the same size, and say which fraction is greater and which is less.

objectives.strand_name: Comparing Fractions and Going Past One
objectives.objective_text: Students share a slab of chikki between two plates, say who has more by counting pieces of the same size, and compare fractions with the same denominator using the signs for greater than and less than.

objectives.strand_name: Comparing Fractions and Going Past One
objectives.objective_text: Students compare two fractions that have the same numerator by comparing the size of one piece, and explain why the fraction with the bigger denominator is the smaller fraction.

objectives.strand_name: Comparing Fractions and Going Past One
objectives.objective_text: Students compare the size of one piece of each paratha, say who ate more when the same number of pieces is taken, and compare fractions with the same numerator using the signs for greater than and less than.

objectives.strand_name: Comparing Fractions and Going Past One
objectives.objective_text: Students join pieces of 1/2 into whole parathas, count the whole parathas and the half left over, and write n pieces of 1/2 as a fraction and as a whole number and a part.

objectives.strand_name: Comparing Fractions and Going Past One
objectives.objective_text: Students join pieces of 1/4 and pieces of 1/3 into whole parathas and pizzas, find how many are left over, and write the total as a fraction and as a whole number and a part.

objectives.strand_name: Comparing Fractions and Going Past One
objectives.objective_text: Students say whether a fraction is greater than 1, equal to 1 or less than 1 by comparing its top number with its bottom number, and explain the reason with pieces.

objectives.strand_name: Comparing Fractions and Going Past One
objectives.objective_text: Students show pieces of 1/2, 1/4 and 1/3 as whole parathas and a part on a number line, add the pieces of the family, and circle the fractions that are greater than 1 in the book's questions.

objectives.strand_name: References, a Puzzle and Revision
objectives.objective_text: Students decide whether a fraction is less than 1, equal to 1 or more than 1, and use 1 as a reference to compare two fractions when one is less than 1 and the other is more than 1.

objectives.strand_name: References, a Puzzle and Revision
objectives.objective_text: Students decide whether a fraction is equal to 1/2, less than 1/2 or more than 1/2 by finding half of its bottom number and comparing its top number with it.

objectives.strand_name: References, a Puzzle and Revision
objectives.objective_text: Students compare two fractions that sit on different sides of 1/2 by finding which one is less than 1/2 and which one is more than 1/2, and say which fraction is greater.

objectives.strand_name: References, a Puzzle and Revision
objectives.objective_text: Students compare fractions using 1 and 1/2 as references, circle the fractions that are equal to 1/2 or less than 1/2, and give the reason from the top and bottom numbers in the book's questions.

objectives.strand_name: References, a Puzzle and Revision
objectives.objective_text: Students follow a family relation one link at a time and name the person at the end of the chain.

objectives.strand_name: References, a Puzzle and Revision
objectives.objective_text: Students name the child's relation to themselves in the book's puzzle and give each link of the chain.

video_coverage.book_item: Book item: Tamanna is a student of Grade 5. She has two chocolates of different sizes. She says that 1/3 of one of her chocolates is bigger than 1/2 of the other chocolate. Is that correct? Explain why this is so.
Book item: When can we say that 1/2 of something is greater than 1/3 of something?
Book item: Shade 1/8 of Grid A in red. Shade 1/6 of Grid B in blue. Shade 1/12 of Grid C in yellow.
Book item: Do you see 1/3 in any of the grids? Mark it.
Book item: Is 1/3 equal to 2/6? Let us find out. Look at the picture and identify the fractions. Are there two different ways to write the fraction represented by the shaded part? ___
Book item: Do you remember how to make a whole with pieces of the same size? How many pieces of 1/5 will you need to make a whole?
Book item: What else is equivalent to 1/2? 1/2 = 2/4 = ___ = ___ = ___

Book item: In groups of 3 or 4, find different ways of making a whole with different fraction pieces from your kit. Write the equivalent fractions for the following that you may find in the process. (a): 1/3 = ___ = ___ = ___; (b): 1/4 = ___ = ___ = ___; (c): 1/5 = ___ = ___ = ___; (d): 1/6 = ___ = ___ = ___

Book item: Find the following using your kit. You can also shade and check by shading. A. How many pieces of 1/6 make 1/3? The shaded part is 1/3. Identify 1/6 in the same whole and find how many pieces of 1/6 fit into 1/3.
Book item: B. How many pieces of 1/8 make (a): 1/4? (b): 1/2?
Book item: C. How many pieces of 1/12 make (a): 1/2; (b): 1/3; (c): 1/4; (d): 1/6?

Book item: Do as instructed using your fraction kit. Make a whole using only 1/6 and 1/12 pieces. Make a whole using 1/12, 1/4, and 1/2 pieces. Make a whole using any five pieces of the same size. Make a whole using any seven pieces. Play in a group with this kit and find other interesting combinations to make a whole. Write or draw your findings.

Book item: Sameer has shaded one-third of the figures. He draws horizontal lines to divide the shapes into more equal parts. Divide the wholes given below into more equal parts and find fractions equivalent to 1/3. Write them in the boxes below the images. 1/3 = 2/6 = 3/9 = 4/12 = ___ = ___ = ___ = ___/24 = ___/36
Book item: The below pictures show 2/5 of a whole. Find the different fractions that are equivalent to 2/5 and write your fractions below each image. 2/5 = 4/10 = ___ = ___ = ___/50 = ___/100
Book item: Fill in the blanks with equivalent fractions. There may be more than one answer. (a): 1/7 = ___; (b): 2/3 = ___; (c): 3/4 = ___; (d): 3/5 = ___
Book item: Put a tick against the fractions that are equivalent. (a): 2/3 and 3/4; (b): 3/5 and 6/10; (c): 4/12 and 2/6; (d): 6/9 and 1/3
Book item: Fill in the boxes such that the fractions become equivalent. (a): 2/5 = ___/10; (b): 3/4 = ___/16; (c): 4/7 = 8/___; (d): 5/9 = 25/___
Book item: Sevi and Shami divided a piece of chikki between themselves. Sevi ate 1/3 and Shami ate the rest, that is, 2/3. Who ate more?
Book item: Compare the fractions given below using < and > signs. (a): 1/4 ___ 3/4; (b): 3/5 ___ 4/5; (c): 5/7 ___ 2/7; (d): 7/8 ___ 3/8; (e): 5/10 ___ 6/10; (f): 2/6 ___ 1/6

Book item: One child says: I ate 4/6 paratha yesterday evening. The other says: I ate 4/5 paratha yesterday evening. Between Sevi and Shami, can you tell who ate more? Use your fraction kit to find the answer.
Book item: Raman's father cuts the parathas into halves (2 equal parts) before serving them. Maa took 5 pieces of 1/2 paratha. How many parathas did she eat?
Book item: Raman's sister Radhika took 6 pieces of 1/2 paratha. How many parathas did she eat?
Book item: Dadiji had 7 pieces of 1/2 paratha. How many parathas did she eat? Find out.
Book item: Raman ate 6 pieces of 1/2 paratha, Dadaji ate 7 pieces of 1/2 paratha and Baba ate 5 pieces of 1/2 paratha. How many parathas did each of them eat? Use the number line to find the answer.
Book item: Maa took 5, Radhika 6, Dadiji 7, Raman 6, Dadaji 7 and Baba 5 pieces of 1/2 paratha. How many parathas were made on this day? Find out.
Book item: Another day, Raman's father cut all the parathas in 1/4. Dadaji took 9 pieces of 1/4 paratha. How many parathas did he eat?

Book item: Raman ate 7 pieces of 1/4, Radhika ate 6 pieces of 1/4, Maa ate 8 pieces of 1/4, Dadiji ate 10 pieces of 1/4, and Baba ate 12 pieces of 1/4 paratha. Use a number line to find out how many parathas were eaten by each of them.
Book item: Dadaji took 9 pieces of 1/4, and Raman 7, Radhika 6, Maa 8, Dadiji 10 and Baba 12. How many parathas were made on this day? Find out.

Book item: Raman's family of 6 members ordered 2 pizzas and cut each pizza into 3 equal slices so that each family member had one slice. Dadiji and Dadaji gave their slices to Raman, Maa and Baba gave theirs to Radhika. How much pizza do each of them have after this?
Book item: Raman could eat only 2 slices of pizza. So, he gave 1 to Radhika. How much pizza does Radhika have now?
Book item: Use parathas and number lines to show the following fractions in your notebook. (a): 2/3 and 5/3; (b): 3/4 and 5/4; (c): 4/8 and 9/8
Book item: Circle the fractions that are greater than one (whole). How do you know? Discuss your reasoning in the class. 7/9, 3/9, 7/11, 9/4, 9/4, 2/5, 4/9, 5/7, 5/4, 7/3, 13/11, 12/5, 12/8, 2/3
Book item: If the length of an ant is 1/4 cm, then what is the total length of 16 such ants walking in a line? Use the number line given below.

chapter_approach.intro: The chapter takes place in a family kitchen. Chocolates, chikki, parathas and pizza are the wholes, and cutting and sharing them shows what a fraction is, when two fractions name the same part, and how to tell which of two fractions is more. A short video explains each idea, and an interactive tool lets the student try it alone.

points.text: Every idea has one short concept video. The tool that follows is where the student explores, builds and checks the idea alone, with hints, retry and reset. Eight tools, each with its own purpose, follow the chapter's own plan.
points.title: Videos teach, tools explore

points.text: Each tool opens with a short recall of the video idea, then lets the student play and apply it, and ends with the chapter's own question, used exactly as the book gives it.
points.title: A tool in three steps

points.text: Every solved example, Let Us Do question and every answerable prompt of the book is its own short video with a step by step solution and a question picture and a solution picture, in a Questions topic that follows the idea it practises.
points.title: Every book question has its own video

points.text: Bars, circles, grids and number lines carry each idea: equal parts with clear cut lines, the fraction as the largest thing on screen, number lines with 0, 1 and 2 labelled.
points.title: The picture is the mathematics

points.text: Grid sizes, bar sizes, kit pieces and every question are the book's own. Any number the plan adds is a practice value and is said to be one.
points.title: Only the book's numbers
